Adult Southeastern blue sucker attain a maximum total length of 59.3 centimeters [Li = 59.3 centimeters], a size that distinguishes them within the Catostomidae family and reflects their adaptation to large, flowing river systems of the Gulf Coast. This asymptotic length corresponds to an ultimate wet weight of 1260 grams [Wwi = 1260 grams], calculated from length–mass regressions derived from extensive gill-net samples collected throughout the Pascagoula and Mobile River basins. Such substantial body dimensions are typical of potamodromous catostomids that require considerable somatic mass to support long-distance spawning migrations. In contrast to many smaller-bodied suckers, the robust physique of this species likely confers advantages in navigating swift currents and maintaining territorial positions in deep channel habitats. The relationship between length and mass underscores a life-history strategy predicated on delayed maturity and substantial investment in structural growth before the onset of reproductive activity.

Females of this species reach the total length at puberty of 39 centimeters [Lp = 39 centimeters], a measurement that corresponds to approximately five years of age based on annulus counts from sagittal otoliths collected during spring spawning runs. This length-based indicator of reproductive onset is an important demographic parameter for fishery managers, as it marks the size threshold above which females are capable of contributing to annual recruitment. The value is consistent with the broader pattern observed among large, long-lived catostomids, where puberty is deferred until a substantial portion of asymptotic size has been attained. At this length, individuals have typically completed the majority of their somatic growth trajectory and begin to allocate resources toward gonadal development for the first time. Tracking shifts in this length at maturity over time provides valuable insight into the effects of environmental variability and anthropogenic pressures on population structure.

Neonates emerge from demersal, adhesive eggs at a remarkably small wet weight at birth of 0.0025 grams [Wwb = 0.0025 grams], a mass that underscores the extreme fecundity required to offset high early-life mortality in this species. This minimal birth mass is typical of broadcast-spawning catostomids that produce large numbers of small, yolk-dependent prolarvae that drift downstream before initiating exogenous feeding. The yolked embryos, which develop within a transparent chorion, undergo rapid cleavage and gastrulation before eclosion, at which point the tiny sac-fry rely entirely on endogenous yolk reserves. The duration of this critical lecithotrophic phase is tightly linked to ambient temperature, with warmer conditions accelerating yolk absorption and the transition to active feeding. Such a diminutive starting mass places stringent demands on habitat conditions during the larval drift period.

Under controlled laboratory conditions at 18 °C [T = 18 °C], the gonadosomatic index (GSI) for reproductively active females reaches 15% [GSI = 15%] during the pre-spawning period. The measurement was obtained from gravid individuals captured during upstream spawning migrations in the Pearl River system and subsequently held in flow-through tanks at stable thermal conditions. Ovarian recrudescence occurs over several months, with the peak GSI being recorded in late winter just prior to the spring spawning ascent. This index serves as a reliable proxy for reproductive readiness and is often used to time hatchery-based broodstock collections.

The maximum lifespan recorded for the Southeastern blue sucker is 33 years [am = 33 years] at 18 °C [T = 18 °C], a longevity that places this species among the longer-lived members of the sucker family. A recaptured individual originally tagged during a mark–recapture study in the Chickasawhay River, with otolith-based age validation confirming the annulus count, supports this estimate. Such extended lifespans are relatively rare among North American catostomids and are typically associated with slow growth rates, deferred maturity, and iteroparous spawning strategies that spread reproductive effort across many years. The capacity to survive for over three decades allows individuals to buffer against years of poor recruitment by repeatedly returning to spawning grounds. This life-history longevity also implies that populations may be slow to recover from overharvest or habitat degradation, as the replacement of older, fecund individuals requires considerable time.
